parts.visual:
A startup needs to launch a feature on Friday to win a $1 Million deal. The engineers write terrible, messy code to get it done fast. They win the deal. A year later, adding a simple button to the app takes the engineers 3 weeks because the core code is a tangled nightmare.

The Code Tax:
1. Technical Debt: The implied cost of additional rework caused by choosing an easy, fast software solution now instead of using a better, cleaner approach that would take longer.
2. The Interest Rate: Just like financial debt, technical debt accumulates 'interest'. The longer you leave bad code in the system, the slower and more expensive all future development becomes.
parts.audio: Technical debt is not inherently evil. Taking on debt to win a massive contract is a smart business decision. The tragedy is when founders forget to 'pay back' the debt, causing the engineering team to eventually grind to a complete halt.

questions.question: A CEO demands five new features this month. The CTO says, 'We can't, we need to spend this month refactoring our old code.' Who is right?
options: It is a negotiation. The CEO is pushing for 'Feature Velocity' (revenue). The CTO is warning about 'Technical Bankruptcy' (the system collapsing). A healthy startup dedicates a strict percentage of time (e.g., 20%) entirely to paying down technical debt.
questions.correct_answer: It is a negotiation. The CEO is pushing for 'Feature Velocity' (revenue). The CTO is warning about 'Technical Bankruptcy' (the system collapsing). A healthy startup dedicates a strict percentage of time (e.g., 20%) entirely to paying down technical debt.
questions.explanation: If you never do maintenance, the car will explode.

questions.question: Listen to the engineer describe the state of the codebase. What is the symptom of massive technical debt?
questions.tts_text: I'm terrified to change anything. Yesterday I fixed a bug in the login screen, and for some reason, it completely broke the payment system. Everything is connected with duct tape. We spend 80% of our week fixing bugs instead of building new things.
options: Spaghetti Code and Fragility. The code is so messy and intertwined that making a change in one place causes unpredictable explosions in another. The team's velocity drops to zero because every action requires massive caution.
questions.correct_answer: Spaghetti Code and Fragility. The code is so messy and intertwined that making a change in one place causes unpredictable explosions in another. The team's velocity drops to zero because every action requires massive caution.
questions.explanation: When velocity hits zero, the startup dies.

questions.question: What is 'Refactoring'?
options: The disciplined process of restructuring existing computer code—changing the factoring—without changing its external behavior. It is the literal act of 'paying down' technical debt by cleaning up the mess.
questions.correct_answer: The disciplined process of restructuring existing computer code—changing the factoring—without changing its external behavior. It is the literal act of 'paying down' technical debt by cleaning up the mess.
questions.explanation: Refactoring is invisible to the user, but crucial to the company.

questions.question: Why do non-technical founders struggle to understand Technical Debt?
options: Because it is invisible. A non-technical CEO only sees the user interface (which looks fine). They cannot see the decaying, chaotic architecture underneath. They often assume engineers are just being 'lazy' when development slows down.
questions.correct_answer: Because it is invisible. A non-technical CEO only sees the user interface (which looks fine). They cannot see the decaying, chaotic architecture underneath. They often assume engineers are just being 'lazy' when development slows down.
questions.explanation: The CTO must translate technical debt into business risk for the CEO.

questions.explanation: The permanent trade-off of software development.
